title: Requiem for a Clinical Trial Participant
subtitle: Jake Seliger is dead, long live the family and data he left behind
body_html:
“I'll call the Director at the ER…just one minute.”

This was Bess Stillman, M.D., the widow of Jake Seliger, as she casually saved my daughter’s life. Bess is a dear friend, and my child had fallen 6 feet, head down onto the concrete, as would later become clear. She had a skull fracture, and it turns out in the emergency room, she was not attached to a level one trauma center. Dr. Stillman saved my daughter’s life, and she’s doing great now, thanks to the excellent decision-making of Bess, , and basically everyone but me, who was pretty useless other than calling Bess in this situation.

Bess and Jake moved to Arizona; you may know him from his writing. You may know her from her writing also: .

Before I go too far, this whole thing is an excuse to tell you about the GoFundMe for Bess and her soon-to-be-child. Donate now.

Jake entered hospice and died last week. Before beginning head and neck cancer treatment, he chose to save some of his genetic material. Bess is seven months pregnant with their child. You don’t have to believe me, but: please, god, internet, take a break from being pissed off about stuff to make sure Bess and her child never, ever have to worry about money.

Jake was enrolled in a number of clinical trials before his death. The data from those clinical trials will save lives. It will inform discussions about risk between doctors and patients. His critiques of the clinical trial system may lead to reform. And his widow, in her day job, saves the lives of people like my daughter every single day. Their daughter’s name has been chosen: Athena. It has been quite a weekend for the data from clinical trials, but one of the things we can't forget? We need to honor those who participate in them.

All of us are dead over a long enough timespan without some of us volunteering to go through potentially horrifying experimental procedures, take medicines that might not work, and sign up to suffer more. Yes, more than anyone would wish— just so all of us might have the opportunity to live a little bit longer when it matters the most. The people who choose to enroll in clinical trials are the reason we get remarkable treatments. Not just those for whom the trial is successful, not just for those who aren't harmed. We need to honor those who don't make it. We need to honor the individuals who didn't benefit. Those who had bad outcomes. Those who experienced adverse effects. Those who died.

It's not just about proving what works; it's about learning everything we can about alleviating suffering in the future so that those who don't choose to enroll in clinical research don't have to suffer for lack of knowledge. Jake made a series of choices that I respect. He made some choices I have made for myself and some I would not.

They also chose to have a child. That child deserves to be loved and cared for, which will undoubtedly happen because of Athena's remarkable mother and father. However, all of us can add a little bit of extra love—right now—a choice we don't often have to honor clinical trial participants at at our disposal.

I’ll leave Jake the last word:

Though having my life cut short by cancer is horrible, I’ve still in many ways been lucky. Most people never find the person who completes them, I think, and I have. I’ve been helped so much. Numerous oncologists have gone above and beyond. Many people, friends and strangers, have asked if there is anything they can do to help. The #1 thing is to support Bess and our soon-to-be-born daughter, Athena, whatever “support” may mean—the most obvious way is the Go Fund Me, as any remaining funds will go to Athena. I wish she could grow up with her father, but that is not an option. Being a single mom is hard;[1] growing up without a parent is hard; I cannot see what Athena’s future holds, except that I think and hope it will be bright, even though I will not be in it, save for the ways in which friends and family promise to keep me alive for her.

Share
